items.topic: Exchange trading vs. OTC trading: trade-offs
items.definition: Exchanges let traders enter and exit positions anonymously and without taking on credit exposure to their counterparty, because the exchange itself becomes the counterparty to every trade. The cost of this convenience is that exchange contracts must be standardized, so only a handful of contract variants exist per commodity.
items.core_idea: Exchanges trade contract flexibility for liquidity, anonymity, and reduced counterparty credit risk; traders use exchange contracts wherever possible and fall back to OTC deals for anything an exchange can't accommodate.
key_points: Exiting a trade on an exchange leaves no residual credit exposure to the original counterparty.
Trading can be done anonymously, including through a broker, whose ID is reported instead of the trader's identity — only the broker knows who initiated the trade.
Exchanges can only support a small number of standardized contracts per commodity to keep liquidity concentrated.
Example: all NYMEX natural gas futures deliver at Henry Hub in south-central Louisiana, so a liquid market exists there but not for delivery elsewhere (e.g., New York City).
The exchange only takes on credit risk between matched buyers and sellers — it does not act as a principal taking a market position.
The exchange protects itself against counterparty default by requiring margin deposits from traders.
Because the exchange only matches counterparties, there is always an equal number of buyers and sellers for any exchange-traded contract.
relationships: Contrasts with OTC forwards/swaps, which trade customization for reduced liquidity and added counterparty credit risk.
trading_implications: Traders default to exchange-traded contracts for standard needs and only pursue OTC deals for delivery points, grades, or terms an exchange can't offer.
A trader wanting delivery away from the exchange's specified hub (e.g., NYC gas) must arrange basis/OTC transactions rather than relying on the futures contract alone.

items.topic: Cash transactions, futures, swaps, and forwards defined
items.definition: The four core energy trade types are cash (spot) transactions and three forms of forward-price contracts — futures, swaps, and forwards — distinguished by where they trade and how they settle.
items.core_idea: Cash trades exchange a physical commodity for cash immediately; futures, swaps, and forwards all fix a price today for a transaction at a future date, differing mainly in whether they trade on an exchange or OTC and whether they settle financially or physically.
key_points: Cash (spot) transaction: exchange of cash for immediate delivery of a physical commodity; 'immediate' is commodity-specific (e.g., within the current month for oil, within the day for natural gas).
Futures: standardized contracts traded on an exchange; result in physical delivery if held to expiration.
Commodity swap: economically a futures or forward contract, but cash-settled rather than physically delivered; traded OTC.
Forward: negotiated directly between two counterparties (not on an exchange); results in physical delivery, like a future.
Swap is a term that means something different in other financial markets (e.g., bonds); in energy markets it specifically denotes a cash-settled forward/futures-equivalent.
Although forwards are theoretically more customizable than futures since they're individually negotiated, in practice they tend to be nearly as standardized as futures.
relationships: Futures = exchange-traded + physically settled; forwards = OTC + physically settled; swaps = OTC + cash settled.
trading_implications: Choice between futures, forwards, and swaps often comes down to whether physical delivery or cash settlement is desired and whether exchange standardization suffices.
common_misunderstandings: Assuming 'swap' means the same thing in energy markets as in other markets like bonds — in energy trading it specifically refers to a cash-settled contract.

items.topic: Common contractual features of futures, forwards, and swaps
items.definition: Futures, forwards, and commodity swaps are all bilateral agreements to buy/sell a fixed quantity of a commodity at a fixed price on a future date, and they share a common set of defining terms.
items.core_idea: Every such contract specifies the underlying asset, the strike (agreed) price, the notional quantity, the settlement currency, the commodity grade/quality, the delivery location, and the expiration date; aside from a refundable margin deposit, none of these contracts require upfront payment.
key_points: Underlying asset: the commodity the contract is based on (e.g., crude oil).
Strike price: the price agreed upon for future delivery/settlement.
Notional quantity: the amount of the commodity to be delivered/settled at expiration.
Currency: the currency in which the buyer must pay the seller.
Grade/quality: the required commodity specification (e.g., crude oil's sulphur content and density).
Location: the delivery point and acceptable delivery method.
Expiration date: the last date on which the contract's obligations can still be transferred to another party.
Other than a refundable good-faith margin deposit, these contracts carry no upfront cost.
relationships: Applies uniformly across futures, forwards, and swaps despite their differing settlement/venue mechanics.
trading_implications: Comparing contracts across venues requires checking all seven terms (asset, price, quantity, currency, grade, location, expiration), since apparent similarity in one commodity can hide differences in grade or location that matter for physical delivery.
common_misunderstandings: Margin should not be mistaken for a down payment or a stake in the underlying commodity position — it is purely a performance-assurance deposit.

items.topic: How exchange order matching and anonymity work for futures
items.definition: Futures are standardized down to a limited set of grades, delivery locations, and delivery windows, and are matched through the exchange's order book without buyer and seller knowing each other's identity.
items.core_idea: Traders submit buy/sell orders to the exchange's book; whenever a bid and offer overlap, a trade executes anonymously, and the exchange then substitutes itself as counterparty to both sides while a clearinghouse assigns the eventual delivery counterparty.
key_points: The exchange fixes delivery time, delivery location, and grade for each futures contract, sharply limiting the number of possible contract variants.
All resting buy/sell instructions are consolidated into a single trading book by the exchange.
A transaction occurs whenever a buy price and a sell price overlap; the two parties never learn each other's identity during this process.
After a trade, the exchange becomes the counterparty to each trader individually.
At settlement/expiration, the clearinghouse — governed by exchange rules — determines who actually delivers to/receives from whom.
relationships: Underpins the anonymity and reduced-credit-risk benefits described for exchange trading generally.
trading_implications: Because counterparties are anonymous and exchange-guaranteed, traders can focus on price/liquidity rather than vetting individual counterparties.

items.topic: Margin: initial margin and daily mark-to-market settlement
items.definition: Margin is a good-faith collateral deposit the exchange requires from every trader to guarantee performance; it is followed by daily cash transfers between traders' margin accounts that track the day's price move.
items.core_idea: Initial margin, posted at trade date and typically sized to cover a large one-day price move (about 5-10% of the commodity's price), protects the exchange against default; daily settlement then transfers cash from traders on the losing side of a price move into the accounts of traders on the winning side, with the clearinghouse administering all the debits and credits.
key_points: Margin is not a down payment and does not represent ownership or exposure to the physical commodity — it is purely insurance for the exchange against a trader's non-performance.
Initial margin size is typically set to roughly 5 to 10 percent of the commodity's price, calibrated to cover a large single-day price swing.

Every day after the trade, the exchange revalues each position against the day's price change and moves money between accounts accordingly (traders on the losing side must deposit more; traders on the winning side receive the transferred funds and can withdraw them).
The exchange's clearinghouse is the entity that executes all margin debits and credits.

Individual traders usually access the exchange through a broker rather than transacting directly with the exchange; in that case the exchange charges margin to the broker, who in turn typically passes the cost on to the client.
Clearing margin (exchange-to-broker) and customer margin (broker-to-trader) are technically distinct but serve the same protective function.
relationships: Directly implements the credit-risk protection the exchange offers described in the exchange trading trade-offs topic.
trading_implications: Traders must be prepared to fund margin calls on unprofitable days or risk having their position liquidated.
Margin costs (including a broker's pass-through) are a real cost of holding an exchange position and should factor into trade sizing/funding planning.
common_misunderstandings: Treating margin as a down payment on the commodity itself, rather than as a performance bond unrelated to the notional value of the position.
